(A nuance)

Abu 'Umar narrated from Ibn 'Uyayna and Sahnun: "The people most bold in issuing fatwas are the least of them in knowledge."

And in a marfu' report mentioned by Abu al-Faraj and others: "Whoever issues a fatwa to the people without knowledge, the angels of the heavens and the angels of the earth curse him."

Malik - may Allah have mercy on him - used to say: Whoever is asked about a matter should, before answering it, present himself before Paradise and Hellfire, and consider how his deliverance in the Hereafter will be, and then answer.

He was asked about a matter and said: "I do not know." It was said to him: "It is a light, easy matter." He became angry and said: "There is nothing in knowledge that is light. Have you not heard the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, We will cast upon you a heavy word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5]? So all knowledge is heavy, and especially that which one will be questioned about on the Day of Resurrection." He also said: "I did not issue fatwas until seventy people testified for me that I was qualified for that." He also said: "It is not proper for a man to consider himself qualified for anything until he asks one who is more knowledgeable than him. I did not issue fatwas until I consulted Rabi'a and Yahya ibn Sa'id, and they ordered me to do so; had they forbidden me, I would have desisted."

He said: If the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ found questions difficult, and none of them would answer a question until he took the opinion of his companion, along with what they had been granted of rectitude, success and purity, then how about us, whose hearts have been covered by sins and transgressions?

Whenever he - may Allah have mercy on him - was asked about a matter, it was as if he were standing between Paradise and Hellfire.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "I encountered people who, if one of them was asked about something, would speak while trembling."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 73, verse 6:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nashi'at al-layl (the rising at night)﴾

Imam Ahmad said:

Qiyam al-layl (standing in prayer at night) is from Maghrib until the break of dawn. And nashi'ah (rising) cannot occur except after a sleep, and one who has not slept is not called nashi'ah.

﴿It is firmer in treading (ashaddu wat'an)﴾

He said: It is firmer in clarity; you understand what is recited and your ear comprehends it.

(Section)

As for al-inshā' (bringing into being, originating), its application to Allah, the Exalted, is only as an act, such as His saying: ﴿And He brings forth the heavy clouds﴾

And His saying: ﴿Then We brought forth for you thereby gardens﴾ and His saying: ﴿And We bring you into being in what you do not know﴾. It is frequent, but the term al-munshi' (the Originator) has not been reported.

As for the servant, inshā' is applied to him in another respect, which is his beginning an action and initiating it. One says: anshaʾa yuḥaddithunā (he began to speak to us), and anshaʾa al-sayr (he began the journey), so he is a munshi' of that. This is a restricted inshā'; the inshā' of the Lord is an unrestricted inshā'. This term revolves around the meaning of initiation: Allah originated (anshaʾahu) him, meaning He began his creation; anshaʾa yafʿalu kadhā (he began to do such-and-such); fulān yunshi'u al-aḥādīth (so-and-so originates narrations), meaning he initiates their composition; and al-nāshi' is the first that rises from the clouds.

Al-Jawhari said: "Nashi'at al-layl is its first hours."

I say: This has been said by more than one of the Salaf, that nashi'at al-layl is its beginning, from which the night rises. The correct view is that it is not restricted to the first hour; rather, its hours are nashi'ah after nashi'ah, whenever one hour ends another rises after it.

Abu ʿUbayda said: "Nashi'at al-layl are its hours and its periods, one rising after another."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Nashi'at al-layl: whatever arises from it, that is, occurs from it, is nashi'ah."

Ibn Qutayba said: "It is the periods and hours of the night," derived from nasha'tu tanshaʾu nashʾan, meaning I began and came forth one thing after another, and Allah caused them to rise (anshaʾahā), so they rose. The meaning is that the hours of the night are nashi'ah. The statement of the author of al-Sihah is transmitted from many of the Salaf.

ʿAli ibn al-Husayn said: "Nashi'at al-layl is what lies between Maghrib and ʿIshaʾ."

This is the view of Anas, Thabit, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Hakam, and the preference of al-Kisai.

They said: "Nashi'at al-layl is its beginning."

These scholars took into account the meaning of priority in the word nāshi'a.

There is a third view: that the entire night is nashi'ah. This is the view of ʿIkrima, Abu Mijlaz, Mujahid, al-Suddi, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration.

Ibn Abi Mulayka said: "I asked Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn ʿAbbas about nashi'at al-layl, and they both said: 'The whole night is nashi'ah.'"

These are the views of those who made nashi'at al-layl a period of time. As for those who made it an act that arises at night, nashi'ah for them is a name for what is done at night of standing in prayer.

This is the view of Ibn Masʿud, Muʿawiya ibn Qurra, and a group who said: "Nashi'at al-layl is qiyam al-layl." Others, including ʿA'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said that standing in prayer is only nashi'ah if it is preceded by sleep.

ʿA'isha said: "Nashi'at al-layl is standing in prayer after sleep."

This is the view of Ibn al-A'rabi, who said: "If you sleep at the beginning of the night a sleep and then stand up, that is the nash'a (rising)."

And from this comes nashi'at al-layl.

According to the view of the first group, the phrase nashi'at al-layl is in the sense of attributing a species to its genus, meaning a rising from it. According to the view of these others, the idafa is in the sense of "in," meaning an act arising in it.

The point is that inshā' is initiation, whether it is preceded by its like, as in the second creation (al-nash'a al-thāniya), or not preceded by it, as in the first creation (al-nash'a al-ūlā).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 73, verse 8 (part 1 of 2):**

Al-tabattul (exclusive devotion) is al-inqita' (severing oneself, detachment). It is a form of *tafa''ul* derived from *al-batl*, which means cutting off.

Maryam, peace be upon her, was called *al-Batul* because she cut herself off from husbands and from having equals among the women of her time. She therefore surpassed the women of her age in nobility and virtue, and she was set apart from them.

The verbal noun of *battala* (*tabattul*) is like *ta'allum* and *tafahhum*, but it has come in the form of *tafil*, the verbal noun of *tafa''ala*, for a subtle secret.

In this form there is an indication of gradualness, effort, deliberate striving, multiplicity and intensification. The verb conveys one of these meanings and the verbal noun conveys the other. It is as if it were said: "Sever yourself toward Allah with a complete severing, and devote yourself to Him with devotion." Thus both meanings are understood from the verb and its verbal noun. This is common in the Qur'an, and it is among the finest forms of brevity and conciseness.

**(Benefits and admonitions)**

Between the servant and Allah and Paradise there is a bridge that is crossed by two steps: a step away from one's self and a step away from creation. He lets go of his self and nullifies it in his dealings with people, and he lets go of people and nullifies them in his dealings with Allah. He turns only to the one who guided him to Allah and to the path that leads to Him.

A preacher cried out to the Companions: ﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near for them﴾. Their hearts were seized with fear, and eyes flowed with tears out of caution. ﴿So the valleys flowed with their measure﴾.

The world adorned itself for ʿAli, so he said: "You are divorced three times; I have no right of return to you." One pronouncement would have sufficed under the Sunnah, but he combined the three so that desire would not imagine that returning to her was permissible. His sound religion and upright nature refuse the *muhallil* (the one who marries a divorced woman to make her lawful for her former husband). How could he, when he is one of the narrators of the hadith, "May Allah curse the muhallil"?

There is no place of solitude in this abode, so take it within yourself. The attractions will certainly pull at you, so recognize them and be wary of them.

Worldly preoccupations will not harm you when you are free of them, even while you are amid them. The light of truth is brighter than the sun, and it is fitting that the bats of insight should be blinded by it.

The path to Allah is free of people of doubt and of those who follow their desires. It is populated by people of certainty and patience, who stand on the path like banners:

﴿And We made among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and were certain of Our signs﴾.

**[Section: The station of tabattul]**

Among the stations of ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of *tabattul*.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 8].

The author of *al-Manazil* (Ansari al-Harawi) said:

Tabattul is severing oneself toward Allah completely.

His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿To Him is the true call﴾ [al-Ra'd: 14] means pure *tajrid* (stripping away of all else).

By pure *tajrid* he means devotion free of looking for compensation, such that the one devoted is not like a hired worker who serves only for wages. When he receives his wages, he leaves the employer's door. The servant, by contrast, serves out of the obligation of his servitude, not for pay. He does not leave his master's door unless he is a runaway. The runaway has left the honor of servitude and has not attained the freedom of release. Thus he becomes despised before his master and before his fellow servants. The highest honor of the soul is to enter the bondage of servitude willingly, by choice and out of love, not unwillingly and by compulsion.

As it has been said:

*The honor of souls is entering their bondage,*
*and the slave takes pride in being owned.*

The reason the verse ﴿To Him is the true call﴾ is well cited here is to express this meaning: that He, the Exalted, is the owner of the true call by virtue of His essence and attributes, even if He does not make the one who calls to Him deserving of reward by it. He deserves it by His very essence. He is worthy to be worshipped alone, called upon alone, sought, thanked and praised, loved, hoped in, and feared, relied upon, sought for help, sought for refuge, turned to, and aimed at. Thus the divine call of truth belongs to Him alone.

Whoever has this established in his heart, through knowledge, experience and state, is rightly granted the station of *tabattul* and pure *tajrid*.

The early generation (*salaf*) interpreted "the call of truth" as monotheism, sincerity in it, and truthfulness. This is what they meant.

ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The call of truth is tawhid."

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "It is the testimony that there is no god but Allah."

It was also said: it is supplication with sincerity, and sincere supplication is only for Allah.

The call of truth is the call to divinity, its rights, its purity and its sincerity.

**[The first degree: stripping away severance from portions and attention to the world]**

He said: it has three degrees.

The first degree: stripping the severing from portions (*hudhuz*, personal shares and gains) and from attention to the world, whether out of fear, hope, or concern for any state.

I say: *tabattul* combines two matters, connection and disconnection, and it is not valid without both.

Disconnection is the severing of the heart from the portions of the self that compete with the Lord's purpose for him, and from the heart's turning toward anything other than Allah, whether out of fear of it, desire for it, concern for it, or thinking about it, such that the heart is occupied away from Allah.

Connection is not valid except after this disconnection. It is the heart's connection to Allah, its turning to Him, and the directing of its face toward Him, in love, fear, hope, repentance and reliance.

Then the Shaykh mentioned what helps with this *tajrid* and by what means it is attained. He said:

By cutting off hope through contentment, cutting off fear through submission, and rejecting concern through witnessing the Truth.

He means: what cuts off the root of hope in creatures from your heart is contentment with the judgment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and with His apportionment for you. Whoever is content with Allah's judgment and apportionment, no place remains in his heart for hope in creatures.

What cuts off the root of fear is submission to Allah. Whoever submits to Allah and surrenders to Him, and knows that what befell him would not have missed him, and what missed him would not have befallen him, and knows that nothing will strike him except what Allah has written for him, no place remains in his heart for fear of creatures either.

His soul, for which he fears, he has entrusted to its Protector and Master. He knows that nothing will strike it except what has been written for it, and that what has been written for it must reach it.

So there is no meaning to fear of anyone other than Allah in any respect.

In submission there is also a subtle benefit: when Allah accepts it, He has deposited it with Himself, secured it in His safekeeping, and placed it under His protection, where the hand of an enemy transgressor cannot reach it, nor the oppression of a tyrant who exceeds bounds.

What cuts off the root of concern for people is witnessing the Truth. This is the vision of all things as from Allah, through Allah, in His grip, and under His subjugation and authority. Nothing among them moves except by His power and might. Nothing benefits or harms except by His permission and will.

So what is the point of concern for creatures after this witnessing?

**[The second degree: stripping away severance from attention to the self by avoiding desire]**

He said: the second degree is stripping the severance from attention to the self through avoiding desire,

and by breathing the fragrance of the spirit of intimacy, and by catching the glimmer of the lightning of unveiling.

The difference between this degree and the one before it is that the first is severance from creation, and this one is severance from the self. He made it three things:

The first: avoiding desire, opposing it, and forbidding the self from it, because following it prevents *tabattul*.

The second, which comes after opposing desire: breathing the fragrance of the spirit of intimacy with Allah. The spirit is to the soul what the spirit is to the body; it is its life and its ease.

This spirit only comes to him when he turns away from his desire. Then he breathes the fragrance of the spirit of intimacy with Allah and finds its scent, for the soul must have some attachment. When its attachment to its desire is severed, it finds the spirit of intimacy with Allah, and its breezes blow over it, refreshing it and giving it life.

The third: catching the glimmer of the lightning of unveiling. This is looking at it, watching for it, and gazing toward it, so that one may know the places where rain falls and the spots where mercy descends.

By unveiling here he does not mean the lowly partial unveiling, which is shared by the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, such as unveiling people's hidden secrets and concealed matters. Rather he means unveiling of three things, which are the furthest reach of the unveiling of the truthful, the people of insight:

The first: unveiling of the stations of the journey.

The second: unveiling of the defects of the self and the afflictions of deeds and what corrupts them.

The third: unveiling of the meanings of the Names and Attributes and the realities of tawhid and knowledge.

These three realms are the principal sciences of the people of the path. Around them they circle, about them they hum, and toward them they strive. Among them is one whose speech is mostly about the journey and the description of the stations. Among them is one whose speech is mostly about the afflictions and obstacles. Among them is one whose speech is mostly about tawhid and knowledge and the realities of the Names and Attributes.

The truthful and intelligent seeker takes from each of them the truth that he has, and uses it to achieve his aim. He does not reject the truth he finds with one of them because of another's shortcoming in a different truth, nor does he waste it. The absolute perfection belongs to Allah, the Lord of the worlds, and no servant is without a known station.

**[The third degree: stripping the severance toward precedence through rectifying uprightness]**

He said: the third degree is stripping the severance toward precedence through rectifying uprightness, through being absorbed in the intention of arrival, and through looking at the first stages of unification.

When he made the first degree a severance from creation and the second a severance from the self, he made the third a striving for precedence. He made it through rectifying uprightness, which is turning away from everything other than the Truth, adhering to turning toward Him, and occupying oneself with what He loves. Then comes being absorbed in the intention of arrival.

This is when the desire to arrive occupies him to the exclusion of everything else, so that it absorbs his concerns, his resolutions, his will and his times. This occurs only after the flash of unveiling mentioned above has appeared to him.

As for looking at the first stages of unification: unification (*jam'*) is the standing of all creation by the Truth alone, and His standing over them through lordship and governance.

Looking at the first stages of this is turning to its preliminaries and beginnings. These are the ascent from which one descends into the valley of annihilation (*fana'*).

It has been said: it is a halt that confronts the one who cuts through the valleys of separation (*farq*) before he reaches unification, and from it he gazes down upon it.

This halt confronts every seeker of glory in his quest. From it he either turns back on his heels, or reaches his goal, as has been said:

*The lover must have a pause,*
*between consolation and passion...*
*And there he moves his feet, either backward or forward.*

What appears to me from his words is that the first stages of unification are its beginnings, its gleams and its flashes.

After this there is a fourth degree, which is severance from one's own aim from one's Lord, and annihilation from it into the aim of one's Lord from him, and annihilation in Him. So he no longer wants from Him; rather he wants what He wants, severed from every will by Him. He then looks, in the first stages of unification, at his religious and commanded aim, which He loves and is pleased with.

Most of the people of the path say: ﴿You alone we worship﴾ is separation (*farq*), and ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾ is unification (*jam'*).

Then among them is one who sees that abandoning unification is heresy and disbelief, so he turns away from unification toward separation.

Among them is one who sees that the station of separation is deficient and undesirable, and sees the poor state of its people and their scattering. So he turns away from it, working toward unification,

and he goes wherever its mounts go.

The upright among them say: the servant on the path must have both unification and separation, and the establishment of servitude is through both. Whoever has no separation has no servitude, and whoever has no unification has no knowledge and no spiritual state.

So: ﴿You alone we worship﴾ is separation, and ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾ is unification.

The truth is that each of the two witnessings, ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾, contains both separation and unification, and the perfection of servitude lies in fulfilling both in every witnessing.

The separation in ﴿You alone we worship﴾ is the diversity of what is worshipped through, and the multiplicity of its connections and kinds.

Its unification is the oneness of the One worshipped in all of that, the intending of His face alone, and the annihilation from every portion and aim that competes with His right and His purpose.

So this witnessing includes separation within unification and multiplicity within oneness. Its possessor moves through the stations of servitude from one act of worship to another, with one object of worship: there is no god but Him.

As for the separation in ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾, it is the witnessing of that by which one seeks help, its rank and station, its place in benefit and harm, its beginning and its end, its connection, and even its disconnection, and what follows from this connection and disconnection.

Ibn al-Qayyim said:

And he witnesses, together with this, the poverty, need and deficiency of the one who seeks help, and his dire necessity for the perfections which he seeks from his Lord to attain, and the afflictions which he seeks from his Lord to repel. And he witnesses the reality of seeking help (al-isti'anah) and the sufficiency of the One sought for help.

All of this is a distinction (farq) that yields servitude (ubudiyyah) in this station.

As for his unification (jam'): it is witnessing the unique Lord, glorified is He, as the sole doer of actions, and the emanation of all created beings from His will, and their being directed by His determination and wisdom.

So his absence in this station from the distinction that precedes it is a deficiency in servitude, just as his separation within the preceding one without observing the unification is also a deficiency. Perfection is giving both distinction (farq) and unification (jam') their due in this station and in the first station.

Thus it becomes clear that ﴿You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help﴾ includes both unification (jam') and distinction (farq). And Allah is the One sought for help.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 73, verse 9:

God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to take Him as a trustee (wakil). He said: ﴿Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but Him, so take Him as a trustee.﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9].

This refutes the view of some ignorant people who say: that to make the Lord one's trustee is audacity toward the Creator, because tawakkul (complete reliance) requires placing the trustee in the position of the one who entrusts. And that is pure audacity.

He said: Had God not permitted that and encouraged it, it would not be lawful for the servant to undertake it.

This is among the greatest ignorance. For taking Him as a trustee is the very essence of worship ('ubudiyyah) and the pure form of tawhid (monotheism), when its bearer truly fulfils it.

How excellent is the saying of the master of his people and the shaykh of the Sufi path, Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tustari, when he says: All knowledge is a door of worship ('ibadah). All worship is a door of scrupulousness (wara'). All scrupulousness is a door of asceticism (zuhd), and all asceticism is a door of tawakkul.

So what we hold is that tawakkul is broader than tafwid (delegation), and higher and loftier.

(Section: al-Mashriq and al-Maghrib between the plural, the dual and the singular)

Then reflect on their occurrence in the singular in surah al-Muzzammil: since the mention of the night and the day preceded them, He commanded His Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, to stand in prayer at night, then informed him that he has a long stretch of daytime (sabh). When the mention of the night and what he was commanded in it preceded, and the mention of the day and what occurs in it followed, the mention of the East and the West, which are the manifestation of night and day, came immediately after. Their occurrence in the singular in this context is better than the dual or the plural, because the appearance of night and day is one: the day always rises from the East, and the night always appears from the West.

He said in (al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an):

As for surah al-Muzzammil, the East and the West are mentioned in the singular because the intended purpose is the mention of His lordship (rububiyyah) and oneness (wahdaniyyah). Just as He alone is the Lord of the East and the West, so He ought to be singled out in lordship and in reliance upon Him alone. There is no lord of the East and the West other than Him.

Likewise, one should not take any god or trustee other than Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 73, verses 15–16:

That is, how can you deny it, when messengers from Me came before you, bringing good news and warning, and you know the state of those who disobeyed My messengers, how I seized them with a severe seizing?

And he said in (I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in):

He, glorified is He, informed that He sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to us just as He sent Musa (Moses) to Fir'awn (Pharaoh), and that Fir'awn disobeyed His messenger, so He seized him with a severe seizure. Likewise, whoever among you disobeys Muhammad (ﷺ).

(Benefit)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent to Fir'awn a messenger﴾

And it is known that the comparison is in the basic fact of sending, and does not require the two messengers to be alike.
